newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE - Luxury car makers rolling into Egypt market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Luxury car makers rolling into Egypt market.

text.p: A healthy economy powered by investment and privatisation has brought luxury automotive giants racing to set up shop in Egypt.

Last Wednesday, luxury car maker BMW AG opened its first vehicle assembly plant in the Middle East at the Sixth of October satellite city. The Egyptian firm Al Fotouh Company for Vehicle Assembly (ACVA) is the local partner.
The plant is the company's ninth in the world and will initially put together the medium-sized 523i model from completely knocked down kits (CKDs) imported from Germany.
Rival Daimler-Benz AG announced this month that it will start assembling its Mercedes E-200 model in Egypt by November with its local agent, the National Automotive Co (NATCO).
"An American friend of mine tells me Egypt now reminds him of Detroit in the 1950s," says Houssam Aboul Fotouh, chairman of ACVA, referring to the heyday of the U.S. car industry.
"Egypt is now entering a stage that, if everything goes right, the auto industry will boom and that will be excellent for the economy," he added.
INVESTMENT-GRADE RATING

Asian car makers like Suzuki and Hyundai were among the first to venture into the Egyptian assembled-car market in the early 1990s. The French firm Citroen also makes compact cars, which rely for their competitive edge on the high tariffs of up to 170 percent imposed by the government on imports.
A few years ago, the U.S. firm General Motors launched a medium-sized model. Luxury cars have only rolled onto the market since the government began reforming its economy in earnest last year.

"At the beginning of last year Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri came to power and started to change the economy fairly dramatically," says Peter O'Halloran, the Egypt representative of Britain's Jaguar, which opened its first showroom in 1996.
"We felt the market was beginning to open up and decided to to get in. Egypt always had potential and we felt this potential was going to be unleashed during the next couple of years."
Since Ganzouri was appointed last January, Egypt's economy has gained investment-grade rating from international ratings firm Standard and Poor's.

After years of stumbling along, economists say the country's privatisation-led reform programme has finally taken off, earning the approval of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Capital inflows have increased sharply.
MERCHANTS AND BELLY DANCERS
Industrialists say that Egypt's relative stability in a politically volatile region has given global vehicle makers the confidence to get into the market.

"We're very pleased and proud to attract a company like BMW," Ibrahim Fawzy, head of the state-run General Authority for Investment, told Reuters at the BMW 523i launch. "This is a certificate that Egypt is on the right track."
Car makers have for years exported their luxury models to rich and status-conscious Egyptians, in spite of the crippling taxes levied by the government.

BMW says it sold 322 cars last year while Mercedes-Benz, the favourite of produce merchants and belly dancers, says it has sold almost three times as much. Jaguar says it will easily achieve its target of selling 750 cars in the next five years, despite steep price tags ranging from $133,000 to $221,000.

To encourage what it hopes will be the beginning of a car manufacturing industry, the government stipulates that car assembly companies put together their cars using a minimum 40 percent local component. It also reduces the taxes on the CKDs the more "Egyptianised" the car becomes.
GROWING MARKET
The lower tariffs have shaved thousands of pounds off the prices of the locally made BMWs and Mercedes, which sell for $84,000 compared to about $140,000 for the imported model.
Until now, BMW and Mercedes imported all the high-technology parts and the chassis, adding local labour, glass, wheels and upholstery.
But jaded Egyptians, used to public-sector monopolies which showed minimal regard for quality, fear the more Egyptian the car becomes, the worse it will be.
At the BMW plant, however, German supervisors work alongside the labour force, giving advice at each assembly stage and auditing the car thoroughly before it is released.
Egypt's car market is estimated at about 85,000 cars a year and economists say it will grow at about nine percent a year.
DEMOGRAPHIC REALITIES

The German firms are confident the luxury car market will double from its current level of 7,000 cars a year in a few years. But economists say the road to success has its pitfalls -- especially the tax cuts Egypt has to enforce as part of the deal with the IMF and the World Trade Organisation, and its demographic make-up as a developing country.

"What's the population? How many people can afford to buy a car when the per capita income is estimated at $1,200?" asks Ibrahim Hegazy, a consultant and director of the Institute of Management and Development at the American University in Cairo.
"Four percent of the country's 60 million people can afford to buy a car, any car. It's not lucrative to manufacture for the local market," he added.

If the car assemblers want to stay in business in the long term, Hegazy says they must move into manufacturing and then exporting the finished product, like the success stories of the Asian "tiger" economies.
"The future will not be for assembling because there is no value added for Egyptian economy," he says.

"If you develop your own components, produce and manufacture, your feeding industry grows and you will have a very lucrative market because of the labour cost and the geographic position of Egypt. South Koreans are not better than Egyptians," he added.
